text: This chart illustrates the percentage of the population in Mongolia that received a first dose of the COVID-19 vaccine between February 2021 and May 2022. The data shows a rapid increase in vaccination rates during the first few months, rising from 0.09% on February 25, 2021, to over 50% by mid-May 2021. Following this initial surge, the growth rate slowed significantly, with the percentage gradually climbing to approximately 66.88% by May 11, 2022.

This chart illustrates the effective reproduction rate (R) of COVID-19 in Myanmar from April 20, 2020, to January 1, 2023. The data shows significant fluctuations over the three-year period, beginning at 0.46 and reaching a peak of 2.38 on August 26, 2020. Following this peak, the rate generally trended downward through late 2020 before experiencing another notable increase in early 2022, peaking at 1.92 in February before declining again toward the end of the period. Throughout the timeline, the reproduction rate frequently fluctuated above and below the critical threshold of 1.0, reflecting the varying average number of new infections caused by a single infected individual over time.

This chart illustrates the 7-day rolling average of the positive rate of COVID-19 tests in Estonia as a percentage from March 2020 through June 2022. The data shows an initial peak in mid-March 2020, followed by a period of low rates until late 2020, when the figures began to climb steadily. A significant surge occurred in early 2022, reaching a peak above 0.6% in February before declining and fluctuating through the end of the recorded period in June 2022.

This chart illustrates the percentage of the population that received a first COVID-19 vaccine dose from April 2021 through October 2023. The data shows a gradual increase starting at 0.0% in early 2021, followed by a period of steady growth throughout late 2021 and 2022. A significant upward trend is observed beginning in early 2023, with the value rising from approximately 20.82% in January to reach 39.54% by October 2023.

This chart illustrates the steady increase in life expectancy over a period of seven decades, rising from 51.94 years in 1950 to a peak of 82.9961 in 2019. While the data shows a consistent upward trend for most of the period, there is a notable decline in the final two years, with values dropping to 82.2167 in 2020 and 79.4856 in 2021.

This chart tracks the percentage of the population receiving a first COVID-19 vaccine dose from December 2020 through September 2023. The data shows a rapid increase in vaccination rates during early 2021, rising from approximately 0.1% in January to over 70% by September 2021. Following this period of growth, the rate stabilized and remained relatively constant between 80% and 81% throughout 2022 and into late 2023.

This chart tracks the number of new COVID-19 cases per million people using a 7-day rolling average from February 2020 through December 2023. The data shows an initial rise in early 2020, peaking at over 3,800 in mid-2020, followed by a period of fluctuation and a significant surge to over 5,400 in early 2022. After this peak, the figures declined significantly throughout 2022 and 2023, eventually reaching zero from August 2023 through the end of the year.

This chart displays the 7-day rolling average of new COVID-19 tests per 1,000 people from March 6, 2022, to May 15, 2022. The data shows a gradual decline from a peak of 0.05 in early March to a low of 0.02 in mid-April, followed by a period of relative stability where values fluctuated slightly between 0.02 and 0.03 through the end of the period.

This chart illustrates the number of people vaccinated against COVID-19 per hundred of the population from March 2021 to May 2023. The data shows a consistent upward trend over the period, starting at 0.0 in late March and early April 2021, rising gradually through 2021, and accelerating more rapidly throughout 2022. By the end of the recorded period in May 2023, the value reached 19.27.

This chart illustrates the trend of life expectancy at birth over a period spanning from 1921 to 2021. Starting at 38.8 years in 1921, the average life expectancy rose significantly to 54.5 years by 1946 and reached 45.7 years in 1931. From 1950 to 2021, the data shows a generally upward trajectory, beginning at 55.89 years and reaching 74.41 years by 2020, despite minor fluctuations in the final decade of the recorded period.

This chart illustrates the trend of life expectancy at birth in a specific country from 1950 to 2021. Starting at 64.59 years in 1950, the figure generally increased over several decades, reaching a peak of 83.00 years in 2019 before experiencing a decline to 79.02 in 2020 and recovering slightly to 80.37 in 2021. While the data shows an overall upward trajectory with some fluctuations between 1990 and 2005, it highlights a notable recent decrease following the 2019 high point.

This chart illustrates the life expectancy at birth in Nicaragua from 1920 to 2021. The data shows a general upward trend over the century, starting at 24.0 years in 1920 and reaching 73.8368 years by 2021. While the figures rose steadily through the mid-20th century, there were notable fluctuations during the 1970s and 1980s, including a significant drop to 48.6264 in 1972 and another decline in the late 1970s before resuming an upward trajectory into the 21st century.

This chart illustrates the life expectancy at birth in Saint Kitts and Nevis from 1950 to 2021. The data shows a general upward trend over the seven-decade period, starting at 54.43 years in 1950 and reaching 71.68 years by 2021. While the figures experienced some fluctuations and periods of relative stability—such as between 1980 and 1990 and again from 2004 to 2013—the overall trajectory indicates a steady increase in average life expectancy over time.

This chart illustrates the life expectancy at birth in the Marshall Islands from 1950 to 2021. The data shows a general upward trend over the seven-decade period, starting at 52.0572 years in 1950 and reaching 65.2688 years by 2021. While the growth was relatively steady through the late 20th century, there was a period of slight fluctuation and stagnation between 2000 and 2010 before the upward trend resumed in the 2010s.

This chart illustrates the progression of life expectancy at birth in Tonga from 1950 to 2021. Starting at 54.03 years in 1950, the average number of years a newborn could expect to live showed a consistent upward trend over the seven decades, reaching 70.99 years by 2021. While the growth was steady throughout most of the period, the rate of increase slowed slightly in the later decades, moving from approximately 60 years in the mid-1960s to just over 70 years by the early 2010s.

This chart illustrates the life expectancy at birth in Libya from 1950 to 2021, measured in years. The data shows a significant upward trend during the latter half of the 20th century, rising from 33.5863 years in 1950 to over 70 years by the early 2000s. While the figures experienced some fluctuations and minor declines in recent years—such as the dip in 2011 and the slight decrease in 2021 to 71.9112—the overall trend reflects a substantial increase in average life expectancy over the seven-decade period.

This chart illustrates the percentage of the population in Kazakhstan that received a first dose of the COVID-19 vaccine between January 2021 and January 2023. The data shows a steady upward trend starting from 0.0% in early 2021, reaching approximately 46% by the end of 2021, and continuing to rise until it reached 55.98% by mid-January 2023. A notable increase in the vaccination rate occurred in July 2022, where the figure jumped from roughly 49% to over 55%.

This chart tracks the effective reproduction rate (R) of COVID-19 from April 5, 2020, to January 2, 2023. The data shows an initial increase in the reproduction rate, peaking at 1.42 on June 26, 2020, before entering a period of fluctuation and gradual decline that saw the value fall below 1.0 for the first time in late 2020. This chart illustrates the 7-day rolling average of the COVID-19 positivity rate as a percentage of total tests from February 2020 through May 2022. The data shows an initial period of zero percent until March 2020, followed by a significant rise that peaked at approximately 47% in late 2020. After a period of fluctuation and a notable decline throughout early 2021, the rate experienced another surge in early 2022 before declining to a low level of 0.3% by May 2022.

This chart tracks the number of new confirmed COVID-19 cases per million people using a 7-day rolling average from February 2020 through December 2023. The data shows an initial period of near-zero values until April 2020, followed by a series of fluctuations and significant peaks, most notably in late 2021 and early 2022 where values exceeded 180. Following these peaks, the figures experienced a general decline through 2023, reaching levels below 1.0 by late 2023.
